title: "def" creates a function, which is executed when called.
when_to_show: When distinguishing between function definitions and function calls
body: "def" is a keyword used to define a function. Defining a function means creating a named block of code. It’s important to note that just because you encounter a `def` line doesn’t mean the code inside the function is executed immediately. The code inside a function is executed when the function is called by adding parentheses after the function name. For example, even if there is a `print('hi')` line below `def hello()`, nothing will be printed to the screen unless you call `hello()`. When reading code, you should first find where the function is defined, and then check if there is a line where it is actually called. This card is not just for memorizing the meaning of words; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how function definitions, calls, input values, return values, and screen output are connected in actual code. When solving problems, check the function’s contract in the `def` line and follow the order in which actual values are passed in the call line. Next, determine what values the code inside the function produces and whether those values are returned via `return` or simply displayed on the screen via `print`.
detail: `def` is a declaration for creating a function, and the function is actually executed when it is called by placing parentheses around the function name. When reading code, you should first look at the `def` block to see what inputs and processing have been prepared, and then follow the order in which actual values are passed in on the call line. If the function is not called, the `print` statement inside it will not be executed.

title: The `return` statement returns a value to the outside of the function.
when_to_show: When the result of a function is stored in a variable or used in another calculation
body: "return" is a keyword that returns the result calculated by a function to the outside of the function. While "print" displays a value on the screen, "return" sends the value back to the point where the function was called. For example, in `result = add(2, 3)`, when the `add` function executes `return 5`, the entire call `add(2, 3)` is replaced with `5`, and that value is stored in `result`. You can store the return value in a variable, compare it, or reuse it as input for another function. This card is not just for memorizing the meaning of a word; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how function definitions, calls, input values, return values, and screen output are connected in actual code. When solving problems, check the function’s definition on the `def` line and follow the order in which actual values are passed in on the call line. Next, determine what values the code inside the function produces and whether those values are returned via `return` or simply displayed on the screen via `print`. `return` sends a value back outside the function. If you want to reuse the result calculated within a function in subsequent code, you must store the returned value in a variable or pass it to another function. `print` displays the result on the screen, while `return` passes the value within the program’s flow. When reading code, you should follow where the return value goes.
detail: The `return` statement returns the value calculated within a function to the point where it was called. Unlike output that appears on the screen, such as with `print`, the return value can be stored in a variable or reused in other calculations. In the expression `result = add(2, 3)`, you can think of it as the entire `add` call being converted into a return value and then stored in `result`.

title: A "parameter" is a placeholder, while an "argument" is the actual value entered.
when_to_show: When distinguishing between the name inside the function parentheses and the value passed when calling the function
body: "Parameter" and "argument" are terms that are often confused in the context of functions. A parameter is the name written inside the parentheses when defining a function, while an argument is the value actually passed when calling the function. For example, in `def greet(name):`, `name` is the parameter, and in `greet('Mina')`, `'Mina'` is the argument. When a function is executed, the argument value is used within the function as if it were assigned to the parameter name. This card is not just for memorizing the meanings of words; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how function definitions, calls, input values, return values, and screen output are connected in actual code. When solving problems, check the function’s contract in the `def` line and follow the order in which actual values are passed in the call line. Next, determine what values the code inside the function produces and whether those values are returned via `return` or simply displayed on the screen via `print`. A “parameter” is the name of an input used within a function definition, while an “argument” is the value actually passed when the function is called. In `def add(a, b)`, `a` and `b` are parameters, and in `add(2, 3)`, `2` and `3` are arguments. When reading code, you must first figure out how the values passed to the function correspond to the names inside it.
detail: A "parameter" is the name of an input specified when defining a function, while an "argument" is the value actually passed when the function is called. When the function is executed, the arguments are used within the function as if they had been passed to the parameters in order. When reading code, it is important to match the names in the `def` line with the values in the call line.

title: "print" and "return" handle results in different ways.
when_to_show: When distinguishing whether a function only outputs something or returns a value
body: Although `print` and `return` both deal with values that appear to be results, they serve different purposes. `print` is a function that displays the current value on the screen, while `return` is a keyword that returns the function’s result to the point where it was called. If you execute `print('hi')` inside a function, “hi” will appear on the screen, but that does not necessarily mean the function returned a value. If you store the result of a function call that lacks a `return` statement in a variable, it usually contains `None`. This card is not just for memorizing the meanings of words; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how function definitions, calls, input values, return values, and screen output are connected in actual code. When solving problems, check the function’s definition on the `def` line and follow the order in which actual values are passed in on the call line. Next, determine what values the code inside the function produces and whether those values are returned via `return` or simply displayed on the screen via `print`. `print` and `return` handle results in different ways. `print` is output displayed to the user, while `return` returns a value that can be reused within the program. You need `return` to store the result of a function call in a variable. When reading code, you must distinguish between values displayed on the screen and those used in subsequent calculations.
detail: Although `print` and `return` both appear to produce results, their purposes are different. `print` displays output on the screen for the user, while `return` returns a value that can be used by code outside the function. If a function contains only `print` and no `return` statement, storing the result of the function call in a variable may result in the variable being assigned `None`.

title: Variables inside a function are temporary labels used during the function's execution.
when_to_show: When checking how far a variable created within a function is used
body: Variables inside a function can be thought of as temporary labels used during the function’s execution. Since this card serves as a reference for explaining the structure of local variables, it provides a basic model that should be the first thing to come to mind when solving scope-related problems. For example, if you define `total = a + b` inside `def add(a, b):`, `total` is a name that makes the calculation within the function easier to read. While there may be a variable named `total` outside the function, the `total` that is newly assigned inside the function does not always modify the `total` outside the function. At the beginner level, you first look at the function’s definition in the `def` line and check the order in which arguments are passed to the parameters in the call line. Next, you go inside the function to track which values the local variables create and modify. If there is a `return` statement, its value is returned to the calling location; if there is only a `print` statement, the output may appear on the screen but may not be saved as the result of the call. Therefore, when working on function problems, it is safest to list the values separately: the value outside the function before the call, the value calculated inside the function, and the value remaining outside the function after the call. Local variables inside a function are often created anew each time the function is called. If you call the same function twice, do not assume that it continues to use the local variables from the previous call; instead, track each call separately. This card is not intended for memorizing terminology, but rather as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how function definitions, calls, input values, return values, and screen output are connected in actual code. When practicing, create separate tables for outside the function and inside the function, and treat each call as a new table. After writing the actual arguments in the “parameter” column, update the local variables from top to bottom. Finally, check the values displayed on the screen, the returned value, and the value remaining in the outer variable by dividing them into three columns. Doing this makes it less confusing to distinguish which range of values corresponds to a variable, even if the names are the same.
detail: Variables inside a function are temporary identifiers that aid in calculations while the function is executing. Even if a variable with the same name exists outside the function, assigning a new value to it inside the function does not immediately change the value of the variable outside the function. When solving function problems, it is important to distinguish between the value outside the function before it is called, the values passed as parameters, the local variables inside the function, and the return value.

title: Functions allow you to reuse the same rule for multiple values.
when_to_show: When reading a flow where the same function is called multiple times
body: A major advantage of functions is that the same rule can be reused for multiple values. Once you define a rule using `def`, you can call it multiple times with different arguments. For example, `double(3)` returns 6, and `double(5)` returns 10. Although the code inside the function is the same, the result changes because the values passed as parameters are different. When reading code, if the same function name appears multiple times, it’s a good idea to write down the argument values for each call separately. This card is not just for memorizing the meaning of words; it serves as an explanatory aid to help you understand how function definitions, calls, input values, return values, and screen output are connected in actual code. When solving problems, check the function’s contract in the `def` line and follow the order in which actual values are passed in the call line. Next, determine what values the code inside the function produces and whether those values are returned via `return` or displayed on the screen via `print`. To identify reusable code, check whether the same rules are repeatedly applied to multiple inputs. Once you understand the function body, simply substitute different arguments in each call to calculate the results separately. If the function is called repeatedly, you should also verify whether it modifies its internal state or simply returns a value.
detail: Functions allow you to reuse the same processing rules for multiple inputs. Even if the function is the same, if the arguments passed when it is called differ, the parameter values will change, and the result may also differ. If the same function name appears multiple times in the code, you must track the input values, the calculations performed within the function, and the return values separately for each call.

title: When a `return` statement is encountered, the function execution ends at that point.
when_to_show: When determining whether the code following the `return` statement is executed
body: The `return` statement returns a value and also terminates the execution of the function. When a `return` statement is encountered within a function, any code that remains in the same indented block below it is not executed. For example, even if there is a `print('after')` on the line following `return 'ok'`, `after` will not be printed if the `return` statement is executed first. When a `return` statement appears inside a conditional statement, you must verify under what conditions the function terminates early. This card is not just for memorizing definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how function definitions, calls, input values, return values, and screen output are interconnected in actual code. When solving problems, check the function’s contract in the `def` line and follow the order in which actual values are passed in the call line. Next, determine what values the code inside the function produces and whether those values are returned via `return` or displayed on the screen via `print`. When you encounter a `return` statement, the function’s execution ends at that point. Even if there is code below the `return` statement, it may not be reached within the same execution flow. If a `return` statement is inside a conditional statement, the function will terminate early only under specific conditions. For code with multiple `return` statements, you must follow the conditions from the top down to determine which return value is actually selected.
detail: When a function encounters a `return` statement, it returns a value and terminates execution at that point. Even if there is code with the same indentation level below the `return` statement, it will not be executed if the function has already terminated. When a `return` statement appears inside a conditional statement, you must verify under what conditions the function terminates early and whether execution continues to the code below if it does not terminate.

title: A function is defined by its input, processing, and output.
when_to_show: When you need to quickly understand the overall purpose of a function
body: Functions are easier to understand if you think of them as a set of conventions regarding input, processing, and output. Input consists of parameters and arguments; processing is the block of code inside the function; and output is either a return value or screen output. Function names are usually chosen to briefly describe this agreement. For example, `count_items` is likely a function that counts items, and `normalize_name` is likely a function that formats names. When reading code, you must first identify what values the function accepts, how it processes them according to certain rules, and what it returns. This card is not meant for simply memorizing definitions; rather, it serves as a supplementary guide to help you understand how function definitions, calls, input values, return values, and screen output are interconnected in actual code. When solving problems, check the function’s contract in the `def` line and follow the order in which actual values are passed in the call line. Next, determine what values the code inside the function produces and whether those values are returned via `return` or only displayed on the screen via `print`. Think of a function contract as an agreement regarding input, processing, and output. Functions become easier to understand when you summarize what arguments they accept, what calculations they perform, and what return values they produce. When reading code, don’t rely solely on the function name; be sure to check the parameters, conditional statements, and the location of the `return` statement as well. Tests are also created based on this contract.
detail: Functions are easy to understand if you think of them as a set of agreements regarding input, processing, and output. The input consists of parameters and arguments; the processing is the code inside the `def` block; and the output is either a return value or screen output. Rather than just memorizing function names, if you look at what they take in, how they process it, and what they return, it becomes easier to grasp the flow of even long pieces of code.
